# Technical Brief: Compiler Internals Optimization Mechanisms

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm.** The canonical construction (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, Zadeck, 1991) builds SSA form in two phases. First, compute the dominator tree of the CFG, then compute the **dominance frontier** DF(n) for every node — the set of nodes where n's dominance "runs out," formally nodes z such that n dominates a predecessor of z but does not strictly dominate z. Phi-nodes are placed at the iterated dominance frontier (DF⁺) of the set of definition sites for each variable: whenever a variable is defined in block B, a phi-node is inserted at every block in DF(B), and this is iterated because inserting a phi creates a new "definition" that may itself require further phi placement downstream. This produces **minimal SSA** (phi nodes placed only where control-flow merges require them) but not necessarily **pruned SSA** — pruning further requires liveness information, discarding phi-nodes for variables not actually live at the merge point. After placement, a renaming pass walks the dominator tree, maintaining a per-variable stack of reaching definitions, to assign fresh SSA names and wire phi operands to the correct predecessor-specific definition.

**Braun et al. "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form."** This algorithm avoids explicit dominance-frontier computation altogether, instead building SSA incrementally during a single pass over the CFG (suitable for one-pass or on-the-fly compilers, e.g., JIT front ends). It performs **local value numbering** within each basic block (mapping variable to current SSA value as the block is processed) and resolves cross-block reads recursively: when a variable is read in a block with no local definition, the algorithm queries predecessor blocks. If the block has a single predecessor, it recurses directly; if it has multiple predecessors, it optimistically inserts an **incomplete phi-node** (a phi with as-yet-unresolved operands) and recursively looks up the value in each predecessor to fill in operands. Blocks are **sealed** once all their predecessors are known (i.e., the CFG construction has added all incoming edges to that block), at which point any incomplete phis depending on that block can be completed. A separate phi-simplification step removes trivial phis (those whose operands are all identical or self-referential, which collapse to a single value), which is essential for avoiding proliferation in irreducible or deeply nested control flow.

**SSA destruction / out-of-SSA translation.** Phi-nodes are not directly executable; before register allocation and code emission, SSA must be lowered to a conventional form. The naive approach replaces each phi-node with copy instructions inserted at the end of each predecessor block, assigning the corresponding operand to the phi's destination variable. This is where the **lost-copy problem** and **swap problem** arise: if two phi-destination variables are defined with interfering live ranges, naive sequential copy insertion can produce incorrect results — e.g., inserting `a = b` in a predecessor where `b` is itself live-out and used by a parallel phi, causing the original value of `b` to be clobbered before it's consumed ("lost copy"), or a circular dependency among phis in a loop header requiring a temporary (the classic `a,b = b,a` swap, which a sequence of two copies cannot express without a temp). The standard fix, per Sreedhar et al., is to compute copies as **parallel copies** (all phi-resolving assignments execute simultaneously, conceptually) and then sequentialize them correctly using a temporary-variable introduction algorithm that detects and breaks cycles. Coalescing — merging SSA values that are connected by phi/copy edges into the same physical storage location — is done either via **interference-graph-based coalescing** (treat copy-related values as candidates for merging if they don't interfere, akin to register-allocator coalescing) or via **dominance-based / chordal approaches** that exploit the fact that SSA live ranges form an interval structure in dominance order, enabling cheaper coalescing tests than general interference-graph coloring.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis.** Andersen's algorithm (1994) models each pointer assignment as a **subset constraint** between points-to sets: for `p = q`, we get pts(p) ⊇ pts(q); for `p = &x`, pts(p) ⊇ {x}; for `p = *q`, pts(p) ⊇ pts(*s) for all s ∈ pts(q); and for `*p = q`, pts(*s) ⊇ pts(q) for all s ∈ pts(p). These constraints are solved iteratively via a **worklist algorithm**: when a points-to set changes, all constraints depending on it are re-evaluated and propagated, until a fixed point. This is **flow-insensitive** (ignores statement ordering, computes one points-to solution valid at all program points) and typically **context-insensitive** in its base form. Complexity is worst-case cubic in program size (O(n³)) because each pointer's points-to set can grow to include O(n) targets and propagation can trigger O(n) rounds, though practical implementations (e.g., using BDs or sparse bitvectors, as in the `bddbddb` system) scale far better. It is more precise than Steensgaard's analysis because it does not force two pointers that are ever assigned to each other to permanently alias the same set.

**Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis.** Steensgaard's algorithm (1996) instead treats pointer relationships as **equivalence constraints**: whenever `p` and `q` may point to overlapping storage, their "points-to" representations are **unified** using a union-find data structure, merging the two abstract objects into one equivalence class forever (even if, in Andersen's formulation, that merge would only be a subset relation in one direction). This yields an algorithm with near-linear time complexity (effectively O(n) with suitable union-find amortization, aside from input/output size factors), making it attractive for whole-program analysis of very large codebases, but it sacrifices precision: once merged, two variables remain aliased for the rest of the analysis regardless of later distinguishing assignments, producing more conservative (larger) points-to sets and hence more may-alias pairs than Andersen's.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Rather than tracking points-to sets at all, TBAA (as implemented in LLVM via `!tbaa` metadata, and conceptually underlying the C/C++ strict-aliasing rule) assumes that two memory accesses can alias only if their **static types are compatible** under the language's aliasing rules — e.g., in C, an `int*` and a `float*` are assumed never to alias (absent a `char*`, which is special-cased as universally aliasing) unless explicitly unioned or cast through compatible types. The compiler builds a type hierarchy (in LLVM, a tree of "type descriptors" with parent/child "may-alias" relationships reflecting struct field nesting) and alias queries become a type-compatibility check rather than a dataflow computation, making TBAA extremely cheap at query time but unsound in the face of violations of strict aliasing (type-punning via pointer casts), which is why it's gated behind language-mandated UB assumptions and disabled under flags like `-fno-strict-aliasing`.

**Sensitivity axes and array dependence.** Alias analyses are further classified along **flow-sensitivity** (does the points-to set vary by program point, requiring per-point solving, vs. one flow-insensitive summary for the whole function/program) and **context-sensitivity** (are call sites analyzed with separate points-to information per calling context, e.g., via cloning or summary-based context strings, vs. one merged summary for all callers). They're also classified by **must-alias** (guaranteed to refer to the same location — enables strong updates in flow-sensitive analysis) vs. **may-alias** (possibly the same location — forces weak updates/conservative merging). For array-heavy code, alias/dependence queries for loop optimization rely on **array dependence analysis**: the **GCD test** checks whether a linear Diophantine equation derived from two array subscript expressions (e.g., `a[i]` vs `a[i+k]` across loop iterations) has an integer solution by checking whether the GCD of the coefficients divides the constant term — a necessary but not sufficient condition for dependence. **Banerjee's inequalities** refine this by bounding the subscript expressions over the loop's iteration space (using interval arithmetic on the loop bounds) to determine whether a real-valued solution exists within range, giving a more precise (though still conservative) dependence test used to decide whether loop transformations like vectorization or interchange are legal.

## 3. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis.** The Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira (IBM, 1999 PLDI) approach builds a **connection graph** per method: nodes represent abstract objects (allocation sites) and local references, edges represent "points-to" and "deferred" (reference-equals-reference) relationships, discovered via an abstract interpretation over the method body (and interprocedurally via summary edges at call sites). An object escapes if its connection-graph node becomes reachable from a parameter, a static field, a return value, or is passed to a call whose summary indicates capture. This classifies each allocation site into one of (as adopted directly in the HotSpot JVM's EA implementation) **NoEscape** (the object is provably confined to the current method/thread and never escapes even via a callee it's passed to, modulo inlining boundary assumptions), **ArgEscape** (the object escapes via being passed as an argument but doesn't escape globally or to another thread), or **GlobalEscape** (the object is stored into a static field, a heap object outside the method, or returned, and therefore may be visible to the rest of the program/other threads).

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA enabled by EA).** When an allocation is classified NoEscape, the compiler can perform **stack allocation** (bypassing the heap allocator and garbage collector for that object) or more aggressively, **scalar replacement**: if all field accesses to the non-escaping object are statically resolvable, the entire object is "exploded" into a set of independent scalar SSA values, one per field, eliminating the memory allocation entirely and letting each field participate in ordinary scalar optimizations (constant propagation, dead code elimination) as if it had always been a local variable. This is distinct from, but synergizes with, general SROA passes (as in LLVM's `SROA` pass) which operate on `alloca`-promoted aggregates once escape/capture analysis has shown no address-taking survives.

**Synchronization elimination and JIT-specific use.** Escape analysis also enables **lock elision** (also called synchronization elimination): if a `synchronized` block or monitor-enter/exit pair guards an object proven NoEscape (hence thread-local, since no other thread can obtain a reference to it), the compiler can elide the monitor operations entirely, since no other thread could ever contend for that lock. HotSpot's C2 compiler performs exactly this optimization guarded by its escape analysis pass (controlled historically by flags like `-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis`), combining it with **lock coarsening** (merging adjacent synchronized regions) as a related but distinct optimization. More generally, ArgEscape-classified objects can still permit limited optimizations (e.g., avoiding a full heap barrier) even though they can't be scalar-replaced, since their lifetime is bounded by the call even though their identity is visible to a callee.

## 4. Inlining

**Cost-benefit heuristic inlining.** Production compilers use a numeric **cost model** to decide whether to inline a given call site. LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis computes an estimated cost (roughly: number and kind of IR instructions in the callee, weighted by whether they're likely to simplify away post-inlining, e.g., due to constant arguments enabling constant folding) and compares it against a threshold that is itself adjusted by heuristics: calls in a loop, calls to a function with a single call site (trivially beneficial, "inline always" candidates), or cold-path calls identified via **profile-guided data** (block/edge frequencies from PGO, or static heuristics like "this path post-dominates an unlikely branch") get different effective thresholds. GCC's inliner similarly uses an estimated-size/estimated-benefit model (`inline-insns-auto`, `inline-insns-single` parameters) combined with its own cost/badness metric computed from the call graph, including recognition of "simple" early-inline candidates (small, no loops) handled earlier and more aggressively than the main late-inliner pass.

**Call-graph-driven interprocedural ordering.** Inlining decisions are made over the **call graph** (nodes = functions, edges = call sites), and the traversal order matters: **bottom-up inlining** processes callees before callers (so that by the time a caller is considered for inlining decisions, its callees have already been simplified/inlined into their final form, giving accurate size/cost estimates), while **top-down inlining** processes callers first, which can be useful for propagating constant arguments into callees before those callees are themselves considered as inlining candidates elsewhere. Most production pipelines use a primarily bottom-up strategy with special-casing (e.g., "always inline" single-call-site leaf functions early) and must handle recursion by capping inlining depth or using a worklist with revisit limits, since naive bottom-up processing doesn't terminate on recursive cycles in the call graph (SCCs are typically collapsed and treated specially).

**Speculative/guarded devirtualization and inline caches.** For virtual/indirect calls, static inlining is often impossible because the callee isn't known at compile time. **Guarded devirtualization** inserts a runtime type check (comparing the receiver's vtable pointer or class id against a profiled "hot" target) with a fast inlined path for the common case and a fallback indirect call (or deoptimization, in a JIT) for the uncommon case — this is **speculative inlining**, driven by profile feedback showing one target dominates call-site behavior (monomorphic or near-monomorphic call sites). JIT compilers (e.g., HotSpot, V8) implement this adaptively via **inline caches**: a call site is first compiled as a monomorphic inline cache (caches the single observed receiver type), promoted to a polymorphic inline cache if a small number of distinct types are observed, and falls back to a megamorphic dispatch (hash-based or vtable-based) if too many types appear — with the JIT able to re-speculate and deoptimize if assumptions are later violated. **Partial inlining** is a related but distinct technique: only a hot sub-region of a large callee (e.g., its fast-path prologue before an early-return check) is inlined at the call site, with the cold remainder left as an out-of-line call, balancing code-size growth against the benefit of eliminating call overhead on the hot path.

**Interaction with other passes and trade-offs.** Inlining is a key **enabling transformation**: it exposes opportunities for constant propagation (literal arguments become constants inside the inlined body), dead code elimination (unreachable branches in the callee given known argument values), and further inlining of calls that were themselves inside the now-inlined body. This is why inliners are typically run iteratively, interleaved with cleanup passes, rather than once. The fundamental trade-off is code-size growth (which can hurt instruction-cache locality and compile time) against the removal of call/return overhead, improved register allocation scope, and unlocked downstream optimizations — managed via size budgets, growth caps per function, and recursive-inlining depth limits.

## 5. Escape Analysis

*(Already covered in depth under item 3 above — connection-graph analysis, scalar replacement, and synchronization elimination/HotSpot classifications.)*

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**SLP vs. loop-level vectorization.** **Loop-level vectorization** transforms a single loop by packing N consecutive scalar iterations into one vector instruction (the classic "vectorize the loop body" transform, legality gated by dependence analysis across iterations). **Superword-level parallelism (SLP) vectorization** (Larsen & Amarasinghe, 2000) instead looks within a single basic block (or a small code region) for **isomorphic, independent scalar operations** that can be packed into a single SIMD instruction even without a surrounding loop — e.g., four independent scalar additions on adjacent struct/array fields unrolled or written out explicitly. The two are complementary: production vectorizers (LLVM has a distinct `SLPVectorizer` pass and `LoopVectorize` pass) run both, since loop vectorization misses straight-line SIMD opportunities and SLP alone misses loop-carried vectorization.

**Legality and profitability via dependence testing.** To vectorize a loop legally, the vectorizer must prove the absence of loop-carried dependencies that a vector-width reordering would violate. This uses **direction vectors** and **distance vectors** summarizing, per loop dimension, whether a dependence exists between iteration i and some later iteration i+d (distance d, or a symbolic direction `<`, `=`, `>`) for each pair of array accesses, computed via the GCD test and Banerjee's inequalities (see item 2). A dependence distance of 0 or negative in the vectorized direction, or an unknown/unanalyzable one, blocks vectorization (or forces fallback to a scalar loop) unless disambiguated by runtime checks. Beyond legality, a **cost model** decides profitability: estimated vector instruction cost (accounting for target-specific throughput/latency of SIMD ops, memory access patterns — contiguous vs. strided vs. gather/scatter) versus the scalar cost, factoring in **vector width selection** (choosing e.g. 128-bit vs 256-bit vs 512-bit lanes based on target ISA and register pressure).

**Reductions, peeling, versioning, and predication.** **Reduction recognition** identifies accumulation patterns (`sum += a[i]`) that aren't trivially vectorizable because each iteration depends on the previous one; the compiler instead vectorizes by accumulating into a vector register and performing a final **horizontal reduction** (tree-reduce or shuffle-based) at loop exit. **Loop peeling** strips off a prologue of iterations (often to align memory accesses to vector-width boundaries, improving load/store throughput on targets sensitive to alignment) and **loop versioning** generates both a vectorized and a scalar fallback copy guarded by a runtime check (e.g., for pointer aliasing that couldn't be disambiguated statically, or trip counts not known to be a multiple of the vector width). The main loop is **strip-mined**: the original trip count is divided into full vector-width chunks plus a scalar **remainder loop** handling the tail iterations that don't fill a complete vector. For loops with divergent control flow (if/else inside the loop body), **predicated/masked vectorization** executes all control-flow paths as vector lanes with a per-lane mask (derived from the branch condition), merging results via select/blend instructions instead of branching — essential for targets with mask registers (AVX-512, ARM SVE) and conceptually shared with GPU SIMT execution models. LLVM's Loop Vectorizer and GCC's tree-vectorizer (operating on GIMPLE) are the concrete reference implementations embodying all of the above as production passes.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling.** The dominant local (basic-block) scheduling technique builds a **data dependence graph (DDG)** over the block's instructions, with edges for **true dependencies (RAW — read-after-write)**, **anti-dependencies (WAR — write-after-read)**, and **output dependencies (WAW — write-after-write)**, each annotated with the target's instruction latency. A **priority function** ranks ready instructions (those whose predecessors in the DDG are already scheduled) — commonly by **critical-path length** (longest latency-weighted path from the instruction to the end of the block) or by **latency-weighted depth**, preferring instructions on the longest remaining dependency chain so that latency-bound resources aren't idled. The scheduler repeatedly picks the highest-priority ready instruction (subject to resource/functional-unit availability) until the block is fully scheduled; variants include list scheduling in forward (top-down) vs. backward (bottom-up, from the end of the block) direction.

**Trace scheduling.** To expose instruction-level parallelism beyond a single basic block (crucial for VLIW architectures issuing many operations per cycle), **trace scheduling** (Fisher, 1981) selects a **trace** — the most likely dynamic execution path through multiple basic blocks, predicted via profile data or static heuristics, potentially spanning several branches assumed to go the "likely" way. The trace is scheduled as if it were a single large block, which can hoist instructions across branch boundaries. Because this reorders code relative to the original block boundaries, **compensation code** must be inserted on the off-trace (unlikely) paths to preserve correctness — e.g., if an instruction was speculatively hoisted above a branch under the assumption that branch wasn't taken, a corrective copy of that instruction (or an undo) must be inserted on the taken-branch side to ensure program semantics are preserved regardless of actual runtime control flow.

**Software pipelining / modulo scheduling.** For loops, **software pipelining** overlaps the execution of multiple loop iterations so that while one iteration's later stages execute, the next iteration's early stages begin, hiding latency across iteration boundaries (analogous to hardware pipelining, but done by the compiler over loop iterations). **Modulo scheduling** is the standard formalization: it computes the **Minimum Initiation Interval (MII)**, a lower bound on the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations, derived from two constraints — the **ResMII** (resource-constrained MII, based on functional unit throughput and how many of each resource-type operation the loop body needs) and the **RecMII** (recurrence-constrained MII, based on the latency of the longest cyclic/loop-carried dependence chain, since a loop-carried dependency bounds how fast successive iterations can start). The scheduler then assigns each operation a cycle **modulo** the chosen initiation interval, tracked via a **modulo reservation table** that records resource usage per modulo-cycle-slot to ensure no two overlapping iterations conflict for the same functional unit at the same modulo time slot. The resulting steady-state loop body (the "kernel") is surrounded by a **prologue** (ramping up overlapping iterations) and **epilogue** (draining them), a structure sometimes implemented via **rotating register files** to avoid excessive register pressure from the overlapped iterations' live ranges.

**Scope and the scheduling/allocation phase-ordering problem.** Scheduling can be done at **basic-block (local) scope**, or more aggressively at **regional/global scope** (across block boundaries within a function, e.g., scheduling across if-conversion'd regions or superblocks). A persistent difficulty is the **phase-ordering problem** between scheduling and register allocation: scheduling instructions early to fill latency gaps can increase the number of simultaneously live values (increasing register pressure and causing spills), while register allocation decisions (spill code insertion, coalescing) can introduce new dependencies that constrain scheduling. Compilers address this via either running scheduling before allocation, after allocation, or interleaving both ("integrated" approaches) with heuristics that penalize schedules that excessively extend live ranges, but no universally optimal ordering exists — hence it remains a classic unresolved tension in backend design.

## 8. General Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** LICM identifies computations within a loop body whose operands are all loop-invariant (not modified by any iteration of the loop) and hoists them to the loop's **preheader** — a dedicated single-entry block inserted immediately before the loop header, created during loop normalization specifically to give LICM (and other loop passes) a safe, single insertion point. LICM relies on **dominance information**: a computation can only be hoisted if the preheader dominates all uses, and — critically — LICM must respect **exception and memory safety**: an instruction that may trap (e.g., a division that could divide by zero, a load that could fault) cannot be speculatively hoisted above a guard that proved it safe within the loop, unless the compiler can prove the hoisted version can't introduce a new fault on an iteration that wouldn't originally have executed it (relevant to "speculative LICM" variants gated by **loop-invariant guard hoisting**, which hoists not just computations but redundant bounds/null checks proven invariant across iterations).

**Induction variable analysis and strength reduction.** The pass identifies **induction variables** — variables that vary linearly with the loop trip count, i.e., of the form `i = i + c` on each iteration (basic/primary induction variables) or linear functions thereof, such as array-indexing expressions `a[4*i+3]` (derived/secondary induction variables). **Strength reduction** rewrites expensive derived-IV computations (multiplications) into cheaper incremental updates (additions) by introducing a new induction variable that is incremented by the appropriate step each iteration instead of being recomputed from the primary IV each time — e.g., replacing `t = 4*i` recomputed each iteration with `t += 4`. This is typically paired with **induction variable elimination**, which removes now-redundant primary induction variables once all their uses have been rewritten in terms of a surviving IV (or eliminates the original IV entirely if only used for the loop condition, replaced by a comparison against a derived IV's bound).

**Unrolling, fusion/fission/interchange, tiling, and the polyhedral model.** **Loop unrolling** replicates the loop body multiple times per iteration (reducing branch/overhead cost and exposing more instruction-level parallelism and opportunities for scheduling/vectorization, at the cost of code size). **Loop fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into one (improving locality by interleaving their accesses and reducing loop overhead), while **loop fission (distribution)** is its inverse, splitting one loop into multiple to enable other transformations like vectorization on a sub-part that's otherwise blocked by a dependence in the rest of the body. **Loop interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loops (e.g., swapping row/column traversal order in a matrix loop nest) to improve spatial locality when the inner loop's stride through memory is improved by the swap, or to enable vectorization of the innermost loop. **Loop tiling (blocking)** partitions a loop's iteration space into smaller tiles sized to fit a cache level, reordering iteration so that all accesses to a tile's working set happen close together in time — a critical technique for dense linear algebra performance. All of these transformations must respect the dependence structure of the loop nest; the **polyhedral model** generalizes legality checking and transformation search by representing loop nests as integer polytopes (iteration domains defined by affine inequality systems) and dependences as affine relations, enabling systematic, composed sequences of interchange/tiling/fusion decisions validated as a single legality proof rather than ad hoc pairwise checks (as implemented in frameworks like Pluto, Polly for LLVM, or GRAPHITE for GCC).

**Loop-closed SSA and normalization.** Many of the above passes assume the loop has been **normalized** (canonicalized to have a single preheader, a single latch, and often a known-trivial induction variable bound) and is in **Loop-Closed SSA (LCSSA)** form, where every value defined inside the loop that's used outside it is routed through a phi-node at the loop exit block — this simplifies downstream analyses (and transformations like loop versioning or unrolling) by ensuring that all "escaping" loop-body values have a single, unambiguous exit-point definition to reason about, rather than requiring every consumer to trace back into arbitrary loop-internal blocks.

---

# SSA Construction

## Dominance Frontiers and the Cytron–Ferrante–Rosen–Wegman–Zadeck Algorithm

The classical algorithm for converting a control-flow graph (CFG) into static single assignment (SSA) form, due to Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck (CFRWZ, 1991), proceeds in two conceptual phases: computing *dominance frontiers* and then placing φ-nodes at the appropriate *join points*.

**Dominance and dominance frontiers.** A node `d` dominates node `n` if every path from the entry node to `n` passes through `d`. The *immediate dominator* `idom(n)` is the unique closest strict dominator of `n`; the edges `{(idom(n), n)}` form the *dominator tree*. The dominance frontier of a node `n`, `DF(n)`, is the set of nodes `w` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `w` but `n` does not strictly dominate `w` itself. Intuitively, `DF(n)` is the set of join points reachable from `n` along a control path that isn't subsumed by dominance — exactly the points where values defined under different control paths merge, and hence exactly the points needing φ-nodes.

The algorithm computes dominance frontiers efficiently using the dominator tree via the standard recursive formulation:

```
DF(n) = DFlocal(n) ∪ ⋃_{c ∈ children(n) in dom tree} DFup(c)
```

where `DFlocal(n)` captures successors of `n` in the CFG not strictly dominated by `n`, and `DFup(c)` propagates frontier nodes of dominator-tree children up to `n` when `n` does not strictly dominate them. This is computed in a single bottom-up pass over the dominator tree, giving an algorithm that is efficient in practice (the original paper's complexity bound is quadratic in pathological cases but near-linear on typical CFGs; later work, e.g. Cooper, Harvey, and Kennedy's "engineered" dominance frontier algorithm, offers simpler and equally effective reformulations).

**Iterated dominance frontier and φ-placement.** For each variable `v`, let `Defs(v)` be the set of blocks containing an assignment to `v`. Minimal SSA requires placing a φ-node for `v` at every block in the *iterated dominance frontier* `DF⁺(Defs(v))`, the closure of `DF` under repeated application until a fixed point:

```
DF⁺(S) = DF(S) ∪ DF(DF(S)) ∪ ...
```

The standard worklist algorithm initializes a worklist with `Defs(v)`, and for each block popped, iterates over its dominance frontier, inserting a φ-node (if not already present) and adding the block to the worklist if it wasn't already a member of `Defs(v)` ∪ already-processed set. This directly yields what's called *semi-pruned* or *minimal* SSA (minimal in the sense that φ-placement exactly matches the iterated dominance frontier criterion — every φ-node is "necessary" under the dominance-frontier join criterion, though not necessarily necessary under liveness).

**Renaming.** After placement, a second dominator-tree-based pass renames variables: a per-variable stack of reaching definitions is maintained, pushed on definition and popped when the dominator-tree traversal backs out of the subtree, and each use is rewritten to reference the top-of-stack SSA name. φ-node operands are filled in by having each predecessor block push its current reaching definition into the corresponding φ-node argument slot when the control-flow edge is processed.

**Minimal vs. pruned SSA.** φ-nodes placed purely via `DF⁺` produce *minimal SSA* — minimal with respect to the dominance criterion, but this can insert φ-nodes for variables that are not actually live across the join (i.e., dead on all paths past that point). *Pruned SSA* additionally incorporates **live variable analysis**: a φ-node for `v` at block `b` is only inserted if `v` is live-in to `b`. This requires a prior liveness pass (backward dataflow analysis computing LiveIn/LiveOut sets) and eliminates φ-nodes that would immediately be dead, reducing SSA size and the work of later passes (e.g., global value numbering, SCCP) that iterate over φ-nodes.

## Braun et al.'s Simple and Efficient SSA Construction

Braun, Buchwald, Mohr, Zwinkau, et al. ("Simple and Efficient Construction of Static Single Assignment Form," CC 2013) present an alternative that avoids computing dominance or dominance frontiers at all, instead building SSA incrementally during a single forward pass over the CFG (often directly from an AST or bytecode stream), using **local value numbering** augmented with **incomplete φ-nodes** and explicit **block sealing**.

**Local value numbering / `writeVariable`/`readVariable`.** Each basic block maintains a map from source variable to current SSA value (the local value-numbering table). `writeVariable(var, block, value)` simply updates this map. `readVariable(var, block)`: if `var` has a local definition in `block`, return it; otherwise recursively resolve via `readVariableRecursive`, which depends on the block's predecessor structure:

- If `block` has exactly one predecessor, recursively read `var` from that predecessor (no merge needed — this handles straight-line extension without creating a φ-node at all, which is the chief source of the algorithm's efficiency relative to always inserting φs at every merge).
- If `block` has multiple predecessors, a φ-node is created for `var` in `block` *speculatively*, bound locally first (to break infinite recursion on loops), and then each operand is filled in by recursively reading `var` from each predecessor.

**Incomplete φs and block sealing.** The complication is loops: when processing a loop header before its back-edge predecessor has been processed, the φ-node cannot yet be fully populated. The algorithm marks such a φ-node as *incomplete* and records it in a per-block list. A block is *sealed* once all of its predecessors are known (i.e., all predecessor edges have been added to the CFG under construction) — in a single forward traversal this is typically when the control-flow construction routine has finished emitting all branches into that block. Upon sealing a block, all incomplete φ-nodes registered for it have their remaining operands filled in via `readVariable` on the newly available predecessors.

**Trivial φ removal.** This local construction can introduce redundant φ-nodes (e.g., a φ all of whose operands are itself or a single other value). The algorithm applies `tryRemoveTrivialPhi`: if a φ has only one distinct non-self operand, it is replaced by that operand everywhere it's used (including as an operand of other φs, which may recursively become trivial — this is essentially a restricted form of global value numbering applied locally to φ congruence classes). This produces **minimal SSA** without ever computing dominance frontiers; the paper proves the resulting φ-placement is equivalent to the CFRWZ minimal-SSA criterion. It does not by itself give pruned SSA — dead φs surviving triviality-checking still require a separate dead-code elimination pass to remove.

This approach is attractive for JIT compilers and bytecode-to-SSA front ends (notably used in libFirm, and conceptually similar to approaches used in constructing SSA directly from Java bytecode or Graal IR) because it fuses SSA construction with a single linear-time traversal and avoids maintaining explicit dominator-tree and dominance-frontier data structures during the initial build.

## SSA Destruction / Out-of-SSA Translation

Lowering SSA back to a conventional register-based or non-SSA IR (needed before register allocation or code generation in most pipelines) requires eliminating φ-nodes, and naive approaches introduce well-known correctness hazards.

**Naive φ-lowering.** The textbook approach replaces each φ-node `x = φ(x1 from B1, x2 from B2, ...)` by inserting a copy `x := xi` at the end of each predecessor block `Bi` (or along the corresponding CFG edge if the edge is not control-flow-unique, requiring edge splitting / **critical edge splitting** to insert a new block on edges where the predecessor has multiple successors and the successor has multiple predecessors). This "copy insertion along predecessor edges" approach is simple but creates two classical hazards:

- **The lost-copy problem.** If a value used later is overwritten by a φ-related copy before its last use along some path, the value is lost. Classic example: a loop-carried φ `x = φ(x0, x1)` where `x1` is computed from `x` in the loop body (`x1 = x + 1`), and a copy for the back edge (`x := x1`) is inserted at the end of the loop body — but if `x1`'s live range extends past this point (e.g. it's also used by another φ in a sibling structure) the naive copy ordering destroys the needed value. More precisely, the problem arises because copies for different φ-nodes at the same join, or a φ-copy interacting with a definition reachable only along one predecessor, must be sequenced correctly; an arbitrary insertion order can clobber a value before it is read.
- **The swap problem.** When two φ-nodes at the same block effectively need to exchange values along a given predecessor edge (`x = φ(y, ...)`, `y = φ(x, ...)` with both `x` and `y` live-in from the same predecessor), naive sequential copies (`x := y; y := x`) fail because the first copy destroys the value needed by the second. This is the classic **parallel copy problem**: the full set of φ-copies on a given edge must be treated as a simultaneous (parallel) assignment, not a sequence, and must be serialized correctly, generally requiring a temporary register and a cycle-detection algorithm over the copy's dependence graph (treating the copies as a permutation/functional graph, decomposing into cycles and chains, and resolving cycles with one scratch temporary per cycle).

**Sreedhar–Gao style translation and coalescing.** More sophisticated approaches (Sreedhar, Ju, Gillies, Santhanam's SSA-to-non-SSA translation using "φ-congruence classes," and the reorganization into **translation via live-range splitting and coalescing**) convert each φ-node operand into its own temporary and a per-predecessor copy, then merge (coalesce) temporaries that can safely share a storage location/name. Two dominant coalescing strategies:

- **Interference-graph-based coalescing**: build an interference graph over SSA names (nodes interfere if their live ranges overlap and they're not related by a copy that can be elided), then coalesce values connected by φ-induced copies when they don't interfere — essentially the same machinery used in Chaitin-Briggs register allocation, where copy coalescing is applied opportunistically or conservatively (Briggs-style conservative coalescing, avoiding coalesces that would increase the degree of a node past the color count).
- **Dominance-based (value-based) coalescing**: exploit the fact that in SSA, two values can share a name safely if their live ranges, which in strict (pruned) SSA correspond to dominance-respecting subtrees, don't overlap; this uses the dominance relationship directly (two SSA names can be merged if one's definition dominates all uses of both, modulo interference along the specific paths) rather than building a full interference graph, giving more efficient algorithms (e.g. Boissinot et al.'s "revisiting out-of-SSA translation" using a dominance-based, value-based approach with explicit parallel-copy resolution per CFG edge, avoiding the full generality — and cost — of interference-graph construction).

Both strategies must correctly handle parallel-copy sequencing (the swap problem) per edge, typically by computing, per predecessor edge, the exact multiset of required copies and resolving them with a sequentializing algorithm that detects cyclic copy dependencies and allocates the minimum number of temporaries.

---

# Alias Analysis

## Andersen's Inclusion-Based Points-To Analysis

Andersen's analysis (1994) is a **flow-insensitive**, **subset-based (inclusion-based)** points-to analysis. For each pointer-typed variable or memory location, the analysis computes a points-to set `pts(x)` ⊆ {abstract memory locations}, derived from a system of **inclusion constraints** generated from the program's assignments:

- `x = &y` generates the constraint `loc(y) ∈ pts(x)`.
- `x = y` generates `pts(y) ⊆ pts(x)`.
- `x = *y` generates `pts(z) ⊆ pts(x)` for every `z ∈ pts(y)`.
- `*x = y` generates `pts(y) ⊆ pts(z)` for every `z ∈ pts(x)`.

These are *subset* (inclusion) constraints rather than equality constraints — this is the fundamental distinction from Steensgaard's analysis. The constraint system is solved by a **worklist algorithm**: each points-to set is represented (often as a bit-vector or sparse set), and when `pts(x)` grows, every constraint whose left-hand side depends on `x` (e.g. dereference constraints `*x = y` or `y = *x`) must be reprocessed, since new elements of `pts(x)` activate new subset edges dynamically (this is what makes the dereference constraints *conditional* — they only fire for elements currently believed to be in a set, and because sets grow monotonically, revisiting is safe and the process terminates at a fixed point — the analysis is a form of **cubic-time** (or with modern engineering, often near-cubic but practically much better) fixed-point computation over a constraint graph with dynamically added edges, specifically modeled as a reachability problem over a graph that itself grows).

**Complexity.** The classical worst-case complexity is `O(n^3)` where `n` is the number of variables/locations, since each of the `n` points-to-set elements can trigger additional edges, and each edge can be processed `O(n)` times. Numerous engineering advances (Pearce, Kelly, Hankin's online cycle elimination; Hardekopf and Lin's "Ant" and "bddbddb"-style BDD-based implementations; HVN/HRU - hybrid variable/reference numbering for offline simplification) bring this down substantially in practice by collapsing strongly-connected components of the constraint graph (since variables in a cycle of subset constraints must have identical points-to sets) prior to or during the worklist iteration.

## Steensgaard's Unification-Based Points-To Analysis

Steensgaard's analysis (1996) takes a coarser approach: rather than subset constraints, it imposes **equality constraints**, unifying the points-to sets of any two variables related by an assignment. Concretely, `x = y` causes `pts(x)` and `pts(y)` to be *unified* — merged into a single equivalence class with a single, shared representative points-to set — rather than one being included in the other.

This is implemented via **union-find**: each abstract location is a node, and assignments trigger `union` operations merging the equivalence classes of the relevant abstract locations (the classic structure also tags each equivalence class representative with a single "points-to" edge to another equivalence-class representative, giving a quasi one-level type-like structure where unification is applied recursively to targets whenever two pointers that already have differing target representatives are unified — this recursive unification of pointees is essential and is what gives the analysis its "unification-based" character, since it's not merely unifying the pointers themselves but conceptually unifying "the type of thing pointed to").

**Complexity and precision.** Because union-find supports near-constant amortized time per operation (with path compression and union by rank), and the number of unification operations is linear in program size, Steensgaard's analysis runs in **O(n α(n))**, essentially near-linear time — dramatically more scalable than Andersen's. The cost is precision: once two variables are unified, they share one points-to set forever, even if subsequent assignments would, under Andersen's subset semantics, have kept their referent sets distinct. This leads to significant **spurious aliasing**, especially at merge points and in the presence of generic container-like code; Steensgaard's analysis is typically used when scalability dominates (e.g., whole-program analysis of very large C codebases) and Andersen's when higher precision is required and cost is tractable (e.g., smaller modules or as a refinement pass).

## Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA infers aliasing (or rather, the *absence* of aliasing, i.e. **non-aliasing facts**) from the **static type system** of the source language rather than from pointer flow. The canonical example is **C/C++ strict aliasing**: the standard specifies that an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of its own type (or a few excepted types: `char`, a compatible signed/unsigned variant, or a struct/union member), and the compiler may legally assume that accesses through incompatible-typed pointers do not alias.

In LLVM, TBAA is implemented via `!tbaa` metadata attached to memory accesses, encoding a **type DAG** (a tree of "access paths" rooted at scalar types, with struct fields represented as offsets into a parent type node). Two memory accesses are assumed non-aliasing if their TBAA nodes are not transitively related in this type hierarchy (neither is an ancestor/descendant/overlapping-offset of the other within a compatible root). This allows load/store reordering and redundant-load elimination across statements that an underlying points-to analysis alone (which only tracks *data-flow* of addresses) might conservatively treat as potentially aliasing, because TBAA reasons orthogonally from *source-level type discipline*, independent of actual runtime pointer values.

TBAA is **unsound in the presence of type-punning or violations of strict aliasing** (common via `reinterpret_cast`, union-based punning, or `memcpy`-free bit reinterpretation), which is precisely why compilers gate it behind flags (`-fstrict-aliasing`, which GCC and Clang enable by default at `-O2`+) and why it's a frequent source of miscompilation bug reports when C/C++ code violates the aliasing rule it depends on. TBAA composes with points-to-based alias analyses in LLVM's alias analysis infrastructure (via `AliasAnalysis` chaining/`AAResults`) — a query may be refined by multiple analyses, and the result is the *intersection* of what each can prove (if any analysis says `NoAlias`, the aggregate result is `NoAlias`).

## Flow-Sensitivity, Context-Sensitivity, Must/May-Alias

**Flow-sensitive vs. flow-insensitive.** A flow-insensitive analysis (as above, Andersen's and Steensgaard's in their basic forms) computes a single points-to set per variable valid at all program points, ignoring control-flow ordering — sound but imprecise in the presence of strong updates (e.g., `p = &a; p = &b;` — flow-insensitively, `p` points to `{a, b}` even though after the second statement it can only point to `b`). A flow-sensitive analysis maintains separate points-to information per program point (or per CFG node), enabling **strong updates** (replacing, not just adding to, a points-to set when a definite, unambiguous write occurs) at the cost of much higher analysis expense, since points-to facts must be propagated through a full dataflow framework over the CFG rather than solved once globally.

**Context-sensitive vs. context-insensitive.** Context-insensitive analysis merges information across all call sites of a function (one summary per function), which can cause spurious interprocedural aliasing when a function is called with distinct, non-aliasing argument sets from different call sites. Context-sensitive analysis distinguishes calling contexts — classically via **call-strings** (k-limited call-site history) or **functional/summary-based approaches** (computing a function summary parameterized over its inputs' points-to sets and instantiating it per call site, as in Cousot–Cousot style functional approaches or the "BDD-based context-sensitive" analyses used in tools like Doop for Java, which exploit context-sensitivity variants like object-sensitivity and type-sensitivity as approximations tuned for object-oriented points-to precision).

**Must-alias vs. may-alias.** A may-alias fact states that two references *could* refer to the same location on some execution path — used to block an unsafe optimization (if may-alias, you cannot assume independence). A must-alias fact states two references *always* refer to the same location on every execution reaching that point — enabling positive optimizations like redundant load elimination or store-to-load forwarding even when neither reference's exact target is individually known. Must-alias is strictly harder to establish and requires flow sensitivity (and often path sensitivity) since it is a universal (every path) rather than existential (some path) property.

## Array Dependence Analysis: GCD Test and Banerjee's Inequalities

For array-heavy code (loop optimization, vectorization, parallelization), alias queries specialize into **dependence testing** between array accesses across loop iterations. Given two array references with index expressions that are affine functions of loop induction variables, e.g., `A[a*i + b]` and `A[c*i + d]` in a loop over `i`, a **data dependence** exists if there exist integer iteration values `i1, i2` within loop bounds such that `a*i1 + b = c*i2 + d`.

- **The GCD test** checks only the *necessary* condition that the linear Diophantine equation `a*i1 - c*i2 = d - b` has an integer solution at all, which holds iff `gcd(a, c)` divides `(d - b)`. If it does not divide, no dependence is possible (dependence disproved); if it does, the test is inconclusive (an integer solution exists, but it may lie outside the actual loop bounds, so a dependence is only *possibly* present) — the GCD test is conservative in the "may-dependence" direction and cheap (a single gcd computation).
- **Banerjee's inequalities** (Utpal Banerjee) refine this by additionally checking whether a solution to the dependence equation can exist *within the actual iteration space bounds*, by computing extremal (min/max) bounds on the linear dependence expression over the loop's iteration range and checking whether zero (or the required difference) falls within that bound range. This gives a strictly more precise (fewer false "may-depend" results) but more expensive test than GCD alone, and is the basis for multi-dimensional extensions and direction-vector-based dependence analysis used in classic vectorizing/parallelizing compiler frameworks (e.g., in the polyhedral and Omega-test lineages, which generalize this to exact integer linear programming formulations for affine array accesses).

These tests feed into **may-alias** queries specifically for array elements — two array subscript expressions that provably cannot produce equal addresses for any valid iteration pair are must-not-alias (no dependence), licensing loop-invariant code motion, vectorization, or interchange; otherwise the accesses must be treated conservatively as potentially aliasing, directly analogous to the pointer may-alias/must-alias distinction but specialized to affine index arithmetic rather than general pointer flow.

---

# Escape Analysis

## Connection Graph / Points-To Escape Analysis (Choi–Gupta–Midkiff–Moreira)

The IBM escape analysis of Choi, Gupta, Midkiff, and Moreira (CGMM, "Escape Analysis for Java," OOPSLA 1999) determines, for each dynamically allocated object, whether its lifetime (and reachability) is provably confined to the allocating method, thread, or some bounded scope, using a flow-sensitive, intraprocedural-then-interprocedural abstraction called the **connection graph**.

**Connection graph structure.** The connection graph has two kinds of nodes:
- **Object nodes**, representing abstract allocation sites (one node per `new` expression, analogous to allocation-site abstraction in points-to analysis).
- **Reference nodes** (or "field nodes"), representing variables and object fields that may point to object nodes.

Edges are of two kinds: **points-to edges** (reference node → object node, meaning the reference may refer to that abstract object) and **deferred/field edges** (reference node → reference node, used to model assignments and field stores/loads before fully resolving the pointee, analogous to the "deferred" edges in Andersen-style constraint graphs that get resolved lazily). The graph is built by abstract interpretation over the method body, processing each statement (`new`, assignment, field store/load, parameter passing, method return) as a graph transformation rule analogous to Andersen's inclusion-constraint rules, but with the explicit goal of tracking *escape* rather than full points-to precision.

**Escape determination.** A node "escapes" the current method if it becomes reachable from: a return value (**escapes via return**, enabling it to be used by the caller), a static/global field write (**escapes globally**), a field of an object that itself escapes, or a parameter passed to an unanalyzed/opaque call. The classification is computed by propagating an "escape state" through the connection graph edges — any object node reachable from an "escaping" reference node is marked escaping, iterated to a fixed point. Because the connection graph is built per method and then **summarized** at call boundaries (a method summary records how formal-parameter-reachable or newly-allocated nodes relate to each other and to the return value, abstracting away purely-local reference nodes), the analysis composes interprocedurally without re-analyzing callee bodies at every call site — call sites instantiate the callee's summary graph against the actual arguments, analogous to function-summary-based interprocedural points-to analysis.

This is the lineage underlying the three-level escape classification later adopted by production JIT compilers (see HotSpot below): **NoEscape**, **ArgEscape**, **GlobalEscape**.

## Scalar Replacement of Aggregates and Stack Allocation

Once escape analysis proves an object **NoEscape** (does not escape the allocating method or thread), two closely related, enabling transformations become legal:

**Stack allocation.** A heap allocation (`new`) whose result is proven non-escaping can be converted into a stack-frame allocation (or, in a JIT with on-stack replacement machinery, into synthetic stack slots), eliminating heap allocation cost and — critically — removing the object from garbage collection entirely (it's reclaimed automatically on method return via stack frame teardown, requiring no GC tracing). This requires proving not just that the reference doesn't escape the method, but that the object's size is statically known (or boundable) and, for languages/VMs that support deoptimization, that a fallback heap-allocation path exists if assumptions are later invalidated (e.g. via class hierarchy analysis invalidation or deoptimization from speculative escape assumptions).

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRA) / object inlining.** Even stronger than conversion to a stack slot, if the object's fields are all accessed through statically-resolvable paths (no aliasing ambiguity about which fields are touched), the entire object can be **decomposed into its constituent scalar fields**, each promoted to an independent SSA value (an ordinary virtual register/temporary), eliminating not just the heap allocation but the memory representation of the object altogether. This is the compiler-construction analogue of classical SRA for stack-allocated aggregates/structs (splitting an aggregate into its scalar members so each becomes an SSA-renameable value, enabling further scalar optimizations like constant propagation and dead-code elimination on individual fields) — but here the *enabling* condition is escape analysis rather than simply "the aggregate is a local variable," because without proof of non-escape, a reference to the whole object (and hence the need for a unified memory layout) could leak out and be observed by aliased code paths.

## Synchronization Elimination and HotSpot's Escape Analysis Implementation

**Synchronization elimination (lock elision).** If escape analysis proves that an object is only ever reachable from a single thread (it does not escape to a context where another thread could obtain a reference), any `synchronized` block or monitor acquisition/release guarding access to that object is provably redundant — no other thread can ever contend for that monitor, so the lock/unlock pair (and associated memory-barrier/fence semantics) can be removed entirely. This is a direct, high-value consequence of thread-escape information (a refinement of the connection-graph escape classification that additionally tracks whether a node is reachable from a thread-start or thread-shared field, not just whether it's reachable from the current method) and is one of the most commonly cited practical payoffs of escape analysis in managed-runtime JIT compilers, since lock acquisition (even uncontended, via a fast-path CAS) carries nonzero cost from the memory-ordering fence it must enforce.

**HotSpot JVM's escape analysis.** The HotSpot C2 (server) compiler implements escape analysis (based directly on the Choi–Gupta–Midkiff–Moreira connection-graph formulation, adapted to HotSpot's IR) with exactly the three-tier classification:

- **NoEscape**: the object does not escape the method or any thread it spawns; it is visible only within the method's local scope (and possibly passed to inlined callees, which are transparent for this analysis since they're incorporated into the same compilation unit). NoEscape enables both stack allocation/scalar replacement and synchronization elimination for monitors on that object.
- **ArgEscape**: the object escapes via being passed as an argument to another (non-inlined) method call, but is not stored into a static field, instance field of an escaping object, or returned in a way that exposes it beyond the call; the callee is assumed (conservatively, absent more precise interprocedural summary propagation) not to let it escape further. This classification permits some optimizations (e.g., certain allocation eliminations are still blocked, but bounds for alias reasoning are tighter than fully-global treatment).
- **GlobalEscape** (sometimes rendered **GlobalEscape**/"escapes globally"): the object is reachable from a static field, is returned from the method to an unanalyzed caller, is stored into another heap object that itself globally escapes, or otherwise becomes reachable from outside any boundable thread-local scope. No allocation or synchronization optimization is licensed; it must be treated as an ordinary heap object subject to full GC tracing and real monitor semantics.

C2's implementation builds the connection graph during its IR-based analysis pass (operating on the sea-of-nodes IR after parsing and inlining decisions have been made, which is important because inlining *extends* what's visible to the analysis and often converts what would be ArgEscape or GlobalEscape at the un-inlined call boundary into NoEscape once the callee body is incorporated), then applies **Escape Analysis Macro Expansion** to actually perform scalar replacement (rewriting field accesses on NoEscape objects into direct SSA value uses) and to strip `monitorenter`/`monitorexit` bytecodes corresponding to provably-uncontended locks on NoEscape or appropriately-classified thread-confined objects. Because HotSpot is a speculative, profile-guided JIT, escape-analysis-driven optimizations frequently must be paired with deoptimization guards: if an assumption later proves false (e.g. due to dynamic class loading changing callee behavior, though this is less common for escape analysis specifically than for inlining-dependent speculations), the runtime can fall back to a non-optimized, heap-allocated/fully-synchronized path via on-stack replacement or recompilation.
