# Register Allocation

## Graph-Coloring Register Allocation (Chaitin-Briggs Tradition)

The Chaitin-style allocator, originally from the 1981 IBM PL.8 compiler (Chaitin, Auslander, Chandra, Cocke, Hopkins, Markstein) and later refined by Briggs, Cooper, Harvey, and Kennedy ("Improvements to Graph Coloring Register Allocation," 1994), formulates register allocation as graph coloring on an **interference graph** G = (V, E), where V is the set of live ranges (or webs) and an edge (u, v) ∈ E exists if u and v are simultaneously live at some program point and cannot occupy the same physical register.

**Interference graph construction** proceeds from liveness analysis: a backward dataflow analysis computing LiveOut(B) for each basic block B, from which LiveOut/LiveIn sets at each instruction are derived. Two live ranges interfere if one is live-out of a definition point of the other and they are not the same value (the exact def-based rule: at a definition of variable a, a interferes with every variable in LiveOut at that point except a itself, with a special case for copy instructions `a := b` where a and b do not interfere with each other, enabling later coalescing). The graph is typically built on a per-function basis after conversion to a web/live-range representation, where a "web" merges def-use chains connected through phi-equivalent copies.

**Simplify/spill worklist (Kempe's heuristic).** The classical Chaitin algorithm, and its descendant in Briggs' thesis, builds a stack by repeatedly removing ("simplifying") nodes of degree < k (k = number of available physical registers) from the graph — these are guaranteed colorable regardless of their neighbors' colors — and pushing them onto a stack. When no node has degree < k, a node must be selected for potential spilling using a **spill cost heuristic** (see below) and either:
- **Chaitin's pessimistic approach**: immediately mark the node for spilling (actually insert spill code) and rebuild the interference graph, repeating until the graph is k-colorable.
- **Briggs' optimistic coloring**: push the high-degree node onto the stack anyway (as a "potential spill"), continue simplifying, and only decide at *coloring time* whether it actually needs a spill — because by the time colors are assigned (popping the stack in reverse order), some neighbors may have been assigned colors that happen to coincide, or the node may simply have fewer than k *distinctly colored* neighbors despite having degree ≥ k at build time. This is the key Briggs refinement: a high-degree node is not necessarily uncolorable.

**Coloring/select phase**: nodes are popped from the stack and assigned the lowest available color (register) not used by already-colored neighbors. If no color is available, the node is an **actual spill**, and spill code (stores after defs, loads before uses) is inserted, after which the whole simplify-spill-select pipeline is re-run (iterative rebuild), since spilling changes live ranges and liveness.

**Spill cost heuristics**: the classic Chaitin metric picks the node minimizing `cost(v) / degree(v)`, where cost(v) estimates the dynamic execution cost of spilling v — typically a weighted sum of def/use frequencies, with loop-nesting-depth weighting (e.g., multiply by 10^depth to approximate execution frequency), and store/load cost constants. Nodes already identified as candidates for rematerialization (see below) or with low use density but high degree (e.g., long live ranges spanning many instructions with few actual uses, common after unrolling or inlining) are preferred spill candidates because spilling them relieves pressure cheaply relative to the benefit.

**Coalescing**: when a move instruction `a := b` exists and a, b do not interfere, they can be coalesced (merged into one node), eliminating the move. But naive coalescing can increase the degree of the merged node past k, hurting colorability (Chaitin's original aggressive coalescing could cause unnecessary spills). Two refinements:
- **Briggs' conservative coalescing**: merge a and b only if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (i.e., the merged node is still "simplify-safe" in the sense that it won't force a spill it wouldn't otherwise cause). This is a safe, conservative test that never turns a colorable graph into an uncolorable one.
- **George's conservative coalescing** (the other half of the standard "Briggs/George" pair used in iterated coalescing): merge a and b if every neighbor t of a either already interferes with b or has degree < k. This is useful when one of a, b is a precolored register (e.g., a physical register required by calling convention), where Briggs' test is too conservative.

**Iterated Register Coalescing (George & Appel, 1996)** interleaves simplification and coalescing rather than doing all coalescing before coloring (Chaitin) or all after (Briggs' original "coalesce after coloring, undo if needed"). The worklist algorithm maintains four node categories — simplify, coalesce, freeze, spill worklists — and a move-related/non-move-related node distinction. Nodes that are move-related are not simplified (removed) immediately, since doing so would prevent coalescing; instead, once no simplifiable non-move node remains, a conservative coalescing attempt is made; if coalescing stalls, a move is "frozen" (given up on) to unblock simplification. This **biased coloring** aspect means that even nodes that end up not coalesced are, at select time, preferentially assigned the color of their move-related neighbor when possible, reducing residual move instructions. This is the de facto standard algorithm implemented in LLVM's `RegAllocGreedy`'s ancestor passes and historically in gcc's old graph-coloring allocator.

## Chaitin-Briggs vs. Linear Scan (Poletto & Sarkar)

**Linear Scan**, introduced by Poletto and Sarkar (1999, building on Johansson & Sagonas and earlier work in the SML/NJ compiler by Poletto, Engler, Kaashoek), abandons full interference-graph construction in favor of a single linear pass over **live intervals**. Each virtual register's liveness is approximated as one contiguous interval [start, end] over a linear ordering of program points (typically derived from an ordering consistent with a linearization of the CFG, e.g., a depth-first or block-order numbering — this is an approximation since true liveness in the presence of control flow can be disjoint "live ranges," not single intervals, leading to some imprecision relative to graph coloring).

The algorithm sorts intervals by start point and sweeps through them maintaining an **active set** of intervals currently holding a physical register. At each new interval's start point, expired intervals are removed from active (freeing registers), and if a register is available it's assigned; otherwise a spill decision is made by comparing end points — classically, the active interval with the *furthest* end point is spilled (greedy heuristic minimizing total spill since the longest-remaining interval is statistically most likely to conflict with future intervals). This is O(n log n) (dominated by the sort) rather than the super-linear cost of interference-graph construction and graph-coloring/coalescing fixpoints, which is why linear scan is the standard choice in JIT compilers under compile-time pressure: HotSpot's client compiler (C1), early versions of V8's Crankshaft, and LLVM's fast register allocator (`RegAllocFast` / historically available as `RegAllocLinearScan`) all use linear-scan variants, trading allocation quality for compilation speed, which matters when compile time is on the critical path of program startup/warmup.

Key qualitative differences:
- **Precision**: Chaitin-Briggs captures exact interference via the graph, so it can exploit non-interference between a long live range and multiple short ones (reusing the same register across disjoint sub-ranges); linear scan's interval abstraction merges these, often causing spurious conflicts — mitigated by **live range splitting**.
- **Speed**: Linear scan is near-linear and avoids the iterative rebuild loop of graph coloring (each actual spill in Chaitin requires re-running liveness and interference construction); this is the dominant reason for its use in JITs.
- **Spill quality**: Chaitin-Briggs spill decisions are informed by global degree/cost; linear scan's spill heuristic is local to the active set, generally yielding worse code, acceptable in a JIT's tiered-compilation model where hot code is eventually recompiled at a higher optimization tier anyway.

## SSA-Based Register Allocation

Working on the SSA form itself allows exploitation of a key structural property: **the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form, when combined with the dominance relation, is a chordal graph** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord) — more precisely, it's a subgraph of a chordal graph structured by the dominance tree, because in SSA each value has a single def, and liveness along the dominance tree gives the interference graph properties closely tied to the structure of **interval/comparability graphs**. This result is due independently to Brisk et al. and formally characterized by Hack, Grund, and Goos ("Register Allocation for Programs in SSA Form," 2006) and by Pereira and Palsberg ("Register Allocation via Coloring of Chordal Graphs," 2005, APLAS).

**Chordal graphs are perfectly colorable in polynomial time** via a greedy coloring in a **perfect elimination ordering** (obtainable via maximum cardinality search, MCS), with no need for the heuristic simplify/spill iteration of Chaitin-Briggs — if the chromatic number ≤ k, a valid k-coloring is found directly, exactly and in linear/near-linear time (no NP-hardness obstacle, since general graph coloring's NP-hardness does not apply to chordal graphs). This gives the SSA-based approach its appeal: **allocation and coalescing-adjacent decisions become combinatorially tractable**, in contrast to Chaitin-Briggs where even testing k-colorability is NP-complete in general and handled only heuristically.

**Hack/Grund/Goos pipeline**: (1) compute liveness on SSA form; (2) perform register assignment on the dominance tree using the chordal property — assign colors top-down along the dominance tree, where a child's assignment is constrained only by values live at that point (since SSA dominance ensures a def dominates all uses, the local coloring constraint set at any point is a clique, and cliques nest according to the tree structure); (3) if the maximum register pressure at any program point exceeds k, spill (reduce pressure) *before* coloring, via a separate spilling pass (e.g., based on Belady's MIN-like furthest-next-use heuristics, as used in the SSA allocator used in LLVM experiments and in production in some LLVM backends' "greedy" / basic frameworks that borrow SSA-era ideas) — this cleanly **decouples spilling from coloring**, unlike Chaitin-Briggs where spill decisions emerge from failed coloring attempts.

**The "puzzle solving" subproblem (Hack et al., also elaborated by Pereira & Palsberg)** arises specifically at control-flow merge points (phi-functions / basic block boundaries with multiple predecessors) where the register assignments coming from different predecessors must be reconciled: this is modeled as a problem of permuting values among register and memory locations, i.e., solving a **permutation/parallel-copy problem** — essentially finding a minimal sequence of register-to-register moves (and possibly one scratch register/swap operation) to transform one assignment of values to registers into another, analogous to solving a sliding-puzzle/permutation-cycle problem. This is handled via decomposing the required permutation into its cycles and using XOR-swap-like sequences or a free temporary register when available.

**Coalescing out of SSA**: after SSA-based coloring, φ-functions must be eliminated (SSA destruction), which naively inserts copy instructions at block boundaries for each φ operand. The role of coalescing here is to minimize these inserted copies by assigning the same physical register to a φ-destination and (where safe, i.e., non-interfering) to the corresponding operands — effectively merging the live ranges across the copies, structurally similar to Briggs/George coalescing but applied in the specific context of φ-webs; this is sometimes called "coalescing-based SSA elimination" and is a core concern in Boissinot et al.'s work on fast liveness and SSA out-of-conversion ("Revisiting Out-of-SSA Translation for Correctness, Code Quality, and Efficiency," 2009).

## Spilling, Splitting, and Rematerialization

**Spilling** stores a live range's value to memory (stack slot) and reloads it at each use, converting a register-resident value to one with (possibly multiple) short, memory-anchored sub-live-ranges; in Chaitin-Briggs, a spilled node's live range is "split" into tiny ranges around each use/def after spill-code insertion, which is itself a crude form of live-range splitting that often enables successful recoloring on the next iteration.

**Live range splitting** generalizes this deliberately: rather than fully spilling a value, its live range is divided at chosen program points into sub-ranges, each independently assignable to a (possibly different) register or to a spill slot; this reduces the apparent degree of the corresponding interference-graph node and is central to LLVM's `RegAllocGreedy`, which treats allocation as an interval-based process with an explicit **split heuristic** stage (region splitting, local splitting, and "last chance" splitting at loop boundaries) interleaved with its own priority-queue-driven coloring, essentially hybridizing linear-scan-like interval mechanics with graph-coloring-informed eviction decisions.

**Rematerialization** (Chaitin et al. and refined by Briggs, Cooper, Torczon, "Rematerialization," 1992) avoids a reload from a spill slot by instead recomputing the value from scratch at the use point, when the value is cheap to recompute (e.g., a constant load, an address computation, a simple arithmetic expression on already-available operands) and recomputation is cheaper than a memory round-trip or when register pressure at the point of recomputation is lower; this requires tracking the original defining expression through the spill decision rather than discarding it, and choosing rematerializable candidates preferentially during spill-cost evaluation (their effective "spill cost" is reduced because the reload is replaced with a cheap recompute).

---

# Instruction Scheduling

## List Scheduling

**List scheduling** is the baseline algorithm for reordering instructions within a scheduling region (classically a basic block) to minimize stalls on a pipelined or superscalar/VLIW machine, subject to the **data dependence graph (DDG)**. The DDG is a DAG (within a block) whose nodes are instructions and whose edges encode:
- **True dependence (RAW, read-after-write)**: instruction j reads a value instruction i writes; this is the only dependence that reflects actual dataflow and must always be respected (cannot be removed by renaming).
- **Anti-dependence (WAR, write-after-read)**: instruction j writes a location instruction i reads; this is a *name* dependence, an artifact of register/memory reuse, removable by renaming (register renaming at the microarchitectural level, or explicit renaming/live-range splitting at the compiler level).
- **Output dependence (WAW, write-after-write)**: both i and j write the same location; also a name dependence, removable by renaming.

Edges are annotated with **latency** (minimum cycles between issue of the source and issue/availability-of-result for the dependent instruction) derived from the target's pipeline model.

The algorithm computes, for each node, often the **critical path length** (longest latency-weighted path from that node to a DAG sink, sometimes called the node's "height" or latency-weighted depth) as the primary **priority function**: instructions on or near the longest path through the DAG are scheduled earlier because delaying them delays everything that depends transitively on them, directly increasing the schedule's lower bound. Secondary priority heuristics (tie-breakers) include: number of immediate successors (favoring instructions that unblock more parallelism), resource contention estimates, and source-order (for stability/debuggability).

Operationally, list scheduling maintains a **ready list** of instructions whose predecessors (per the DDG) have already been scheduled, and at each cycle/step selects the highest-priority ready instruction (subject to resource availability — functional units, issue width), simulating the ready list advancing as instructions complete and new instructions become ready. **Local list scheduling** operates purely within one basic block; because basic blocks in typical code are short (average of only a handful of instructions between branches), this limits available ILP, motivating global/regional approaches.

## Trace Scheduling

**Trace scheduling**, introduced by Fisher (1979, 1981) specifically to support VLIW architectures (the Bulldog compiler for the original VLIW research machines, and later commercialized in Multiflow's compiler), extends scheduling scope beyond a single basic block by selecting a **trace**: a linear sequence of basic blocks predicted (via profile data or static heuristics, e.g., branch prediction heuristics) to be the most frequently executed path through a region containing branches, potentially spanning loop iterations and conditional branches, treated as if it were a single large basic block for scheduling purposes (the trace's internal branches are treated as if they "don't exist" for the purposes of moving instructions past them, as long as correctness is preserved).

Because instructions are moved across the trace's internal block boundaries — in particular, hoisted above a branch into a block that a different (off-trace) control path might also reach, or sunk below a merge point — the compiler must insert **compensation code**: copies of instructions placed on the **off-trace edges** (the side exits/entries not included in the trace) to preserve correctness for execution paths that diverge from the predicted trace. Concretely: if instruction I is speculatively hoisted above a conditional branch B that exits the trace, and I's effect is needed on the off-trace path too, a copy of I must be inserted on that off-trace edge; symmetric compensation is needed when sinking instructions past a *merge* point where another trace joins in, since that other trace didn't execute the sunk instruction. This compensation code can grow combinatorially with trace count/overlap (the "code explosion" problem documented as trace scheduling's chief drawback), and later approaches — **superblock scheduling** (Hwu et al., tail duplication to produce single-entry multiple-exit regions, eliminating merge-point compensation entirely by duplicating code so each superblock has only one entry) and **hyperblock scheduling** (using if-conversion/predication to fold multiple control paths into one predicated region) — were developed as refinements that reduce or restructure the compensation-code burden relative to raw trace scheduling.

## Software Pipelining and Modulo Scheduling

**Software pipelining** restructures a loop so that successive loop iterations are overlapped in time, analogous to hardware pipelining: at steady state, each iteration of the new (software-pipelined) loop body contains instructions drawn from several different original-loop iterations, each at a different stage of completion. The transformed loop has the classic structure: a **prologue** (ramping up, filling the pipeline), a **steady-state kernel** (the repeating overlapped body, which is what actually executes the bulk of iterations), and an **epilogue** (draining the pipeline).

**Modulo scheduling**, the dominant practical algorithm for software pipelining (formalized by Rau and Glaeser, "Some Scheduling Techniques and an Easily Schedulable Horizontal Architecture for High Performance Scientific Computing," 1981; and Lam's influential refinement, "Software Pipelining: An Effective Scheduling Technique for VLIW Machines," 1988, in the context of the Warp/iWarp and later used heavily in Itanium's EPIC compiler and TI's VLIW DSP compilers), schedules one iteration's instructions into a schedule of length **II (initiation interval)** — the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations in the new overlapped schedule — such that the same relative schedule, repeated every II cycles, is legal for all overlapping iterations simultaneously.

**Minimum Initiation Interval (MII)** is computed as the maximum of two independently derived lower bounds:
- **ResMII (resource-constrained MII)**: for each resource (functional unit, issue slot, port) r with usage count U(r) per iteration and capacity C(r) available per cycle, ResMII = ceil(max_r U(r)/C(r)); i.e., the loop cannot execute faster than its busiest resource allows.
- **RecMII (recurrence-constrained MII)**: for each cycle in the dependence graph that spans loop iterations (a "recurrence," e.g., an accumulator `sum += x[i]` creating a dependence from iteration i's update back to iteration i+1's use), RecMII = max over all such cycles of (total latency around the cycle) / (total **distance**, i.e., number of iterations spanned by the cycle's inter-iteration edges). This reflects that a dependence cycle imposes a hard lower bound on how fast iterations can be re-initiated, since a value produced at iteration i and consumed (with carried dependence) at iteration i+d cannot be scheduled faster than the cycle's critical latency divided by d.

MII = max(ResMII, RecMII) is the starting II; the scheduler attempts to construct a valid modulo schedule at II = MII, and if it fails (cannot satisfy all dependence and resource constraints within that II), increments II and retries, typically using a heuristic list-scheduling-like pass per candidate II (e.g., iterative modulo scheduling with a priority ordering by slack, as in Rau's later "Iterative Modulo Scheduling" refinement used in the Cydra 5 and in Trimaran/HP's IMPACT-descended research compilers).

The core data structure for legality checking is the **Modulo Reservation Table (MRT)**: a table indexed by (resource, time-slot mod II) recording which resource is occupied at which cycle-mod-II; when tentatively placing an instruction at absolute cycle t using resource r, the scheduler checks/reserves MRT[r][t mod II], so that two instructions from different (overlapping) iterations that would land in the same resource slot modulo II are correctly detected as conflicting and prevented, enforcing that the single steady-state kernel is simultaneously legal for all the overlapping iterations it represents.

After scheduling, **register lifetimes span multiple iterations** when a value produced in one stage is consumed in a later-starting iteration still executing within the overlapped window, requiring either a statically unrolled kernel with distinct registers per stage, or (as implemented on Itanium/IA-64) **rotating register files**, where a hardware base-register-renaming mechanism automatically remaps logical register numbers each iteration so that one static register name correctly addresses different physical registers across the overlapped iterations, directly supported by the EPIC rotating register file and the `br.ctop`/modulo-scheduled-loop branch instructions in the Itanium ISA.

## Scheduling Scope and the Phase-Ordering Problem with Register Allocation

**Basic-block (local) scheduling** operates within straight-line code with no internal control flow, bounded by the DDG described above, with limited ILP given typical basic block sizes.

**Global/regional scheduling** extends the scope to multiple basic blocks without necessarily committing to a single predicted trace: examples include **region scheduling** over extended basic blocks (single-entry, multiple-exit, as used by Bernstein and Rodeh), and more general **global scheduling** that must track, for each candidate instruction motion across a block boundary, both **upward code motion** (speculating an instruction above a branch into a predecessor block, legal only if the instruction has no side effects that would be wrongly triggered on paths that didn't originally execute it, and doesn't clobber values live on other paths) and **downward code motion** (sinking an instruction past a merge point, legal only if it's safe/duplicated appropriately on all paths into the merge, which may again require compensation code as in trace scheduling, or must be rejected for possible exceptions, e.g., a load that might fault).

**The phase-ordering problem between scheduling and register allocation** is a classic, enduring tension: scheduling for maximum ILP tends to increase the number of values simultaneously live (by moving independent instructions close together, more values' live ranges overlap, raising register pressure), which can force spills; conversely, register allocation performed first constrains later scheduling by fixing physical register assignments, which introduces **false dependencies** — a WAR or WAW anti/output dependence purely from register reuse that didn't exist as a true dependence, limiting the scheduler's freedom to reorder.

Compilers handle this via (1) **pre-pass scheduling then allocation then post-pass scheduling** (schedule first to expose ILP while virtual registers are still unconstrained in number, then allocate — accepting that allocation may introduce spill code that needs rescheduling, hence a cleanup post-pass schedule after allocation to re-sequence around inserted spill loads/stores and newly introduced anti-dependences from register reuse); (2) **integrated/unified approaches**, e.g., treating the problem jointly as in some VLIW research compilers, where scheduling heuristics are made pressure-aware (tracking an estimate of live register count during list-scheduling's priority computation and deprioritizing motions that would increase pressure past the physical register budget, sometimes called **register-sensitive** or **pressure-aware list scheduling**); and (3) in modulo scheduling specifically, the interaction is especially acute since overlapping iterations directly multiply the number of simultaneously live values (proportional to the overlap degree, i.e., roughly stage count), requiring either sufficient physical/rotating registers or accepting a larger II (trading ILP for register pressure) — handled in practice by heuristics like Huff's or Rau's register-sensitive modulo scheduling that bias the II search and the modulo schedule construction to bound simultaneous liveness, rather than treating MII satisfaction as the only objective.

# Inlining

## Cost-benefit heuristic inlining

Production compilers treat inlining as the pivotal enabling transformation for subsequent scalar optimization, and gate it with a cost model because unrestricted inlining causes code-size blowup and I-cache pressure.

**LLVM's `InlineCost` model** (`lib/Analysis/InlineCost.cpp`) performs an abstract-interpretation-like walk of the callee body, simulating the effect of constant arguments at the call site. It accumulates a synthetic "cost" from instruction counts, weighted by expected simplification: branches whose condition becomes constant after argument substitution are assumed foldable and their unreachable successors discounted; loads from constant-folded pointers are assumed foldable; calls that would become direct after devirtualization are credited. The resulting cost is compared against a threshold (`DefaultThreshold`, currently calibrated per `-O` level, with `-Oz`/`-Os` using much lower thresholds, and `OptimizeForSize`/`MinSize` attributes further constraining it). Call sites marked `alwaysinline` bypass the threshold entirely; `noinline` vetoes it. The `InlineParams` structure also encodes a `HotCallSiteThreshold` that is substantially higher, consumed when the call edge is marked hot by profile data (see below). There is also the newer **machine-learning-based inliner** (`-mllvm -enable-ml-inliner` / `MLInlineAdvisor`), which replaces the hand-tuned linear cost formula with a learned policy (TensorFlow/Flatbuffer model) over a feature vector (callee size, loop depth, SC size, etc.) trained to approximate the effect of inlining on downstream code size/runtime — illustrating the general trend of replacing heuristic thresholds with learned cost models.

**GCC's inliner** (`ipa-inline.c`/`ipa-inline-analysis.c`) similarly computes a per-call "badness" metric balancing estimated growth (`inline_summary::size`) against estimated benefit, using `--param max-inline-insns-auto`, `max-inline-insns-single`, and `inline-unit-growth`/`large-unit-insns` to bound total unit growth. GCC's early inliner (within-SCC, limited) runs before IPA, while the main **IPA inliner** operates over the whole-program call graph post-early-opts, using a priority queue ordered by badness, iteratively inlining the best edge and re-evaluating affected callers — a greedy, profitability-ranked analogue to LLVM's per-SCC bottom-up walk.

**Profile-guided hot/cold weighting**: both compilers consume PGO data (LLVM: `llvm.loop` / branch-weight metadata and `BlockFrequencyInfo`/`ProfileSummaryInfo`; GCC: `.gcda` edge counts) to classify call sites as hot, cold, or neutral. Hot call sites get an inflated threshold (more willing to grow code for expected runtime benefit); cold call sites (below `ColdCallSiteThreshold`, often tied to function entry count percentile) are discouraged from inlining or are candidates for **outlining** instead. This realizes the classic code-size-vs-speed trade-off directly as a per-edge decision rather than a global one.

## Interprocedural inlining driven by call graph analysis

Inlining is fundamentally interprocedural: the decision at one call site affects the cost estimate at others because callee size changes after it absorbs its own callees. Compilers therefore process the **call graph**, typically condensed into its **strongly connected components (SCCs)** to handle recursion, and choose a traversal order:

- **Bottom-up inlining**: process leaf functions (callees) first, inline into them from their own callees, so that by the time a caller considers inlining a callee, that callee's body already reflects its own inlining decisions and final size estimate. This is LLVM's default `Inliner` pass behavior under the new PM's `CGSCCPassManager`, iterating SCCs in post-order (callees before callers) so each SCC is "finalized" before being considered as an inlining candidate elsewhere.
- **Top-down inlining**: process callers first; useful when specialization opportunities (e.g., constant-argument propagation) should flow from caller context into the callee before the callee itself is further optimized. GCC's IPA inliner is effectively driven by a global priority queue rather than a strict top-down walk, but conceptually prioritizes edges where caller-side context (constant args, hot callsite) makes inlining attractive.

Within an SCC containing mutual recursion, both compilers impose a **recursion limit**: LLVM's inline cost model tracks the number of times a given call chain has already inlined copies of the same function (`InlineHistory`) and vetoes further inlining beyond a small depth/duplication bound to avoid infinite or exponential expansion; GCC's `max-inline-recursive-depth` parameter plays the analogous role. **Self-recursive inlining** (inlining one or two levels of a recursive call) is sometimes permitted up to a small fixed depth because it can expose loop-like iteration amenable to further optimization, but is sharply bounded.

Call graph updates are incremental: after inlining, the call edges of the inlined callee are spliced into the caller's edge set (edges get "promoted" up a level), and the SCC structure may need to be recomputed if inlining merges previously separate SCCs via newly introduced direct calls (this happens with indirect-call resolution via devirtualization, below).

## Specialized forms

**Partial inlining**: rather than duplicating the entire callee, the compiler splits the callee into a "hot" entry region and a "cold" residual region (e.g., via **outlining of cold paths**, such as an unlikely error-handling block or rarely taken branch identified by `__builtin_expect`/PGO), and inlines only the hot region at the call site while leaving a call to the outlined cold remainder. LLVM implements this in `PartialInlinerPass`, structurally identifying single-exit/single-entry regions dominated by an early-return pattern. This bounds code growth while still eliminating call overhead on the hot path.

**Inlining with cloning for devirtualization**: for a polymorphic (virtual) call site where profile data indicates a dominant target class, the compiler performs **guarded devirtualization** (a.k.a. speculative or conditional devirtualization): it inserts a runtime type/vtable check (`if (vtable_ptr == &ExpectedClass::vtable)`), and on the fast path calls the resolved concrete method directly — ordinarily combined with inlining that resolved call. The fallback path retains the original indirect/virtual call for correctness. LLVM performs this as part of ICP (**indirect call promotion**, `PGOIndirectCallPromotion`), consuming value-profile data on indirect call targets; it is complementary to **whole-program devirtualization** via `-wholeprogramdevirt`/CFI-based type metadata when the full set of possible dynamic types is statically known (closed-world assumption), allowing unconditional devirtualization and inlining without a guard. In JIT contexts (HotSpot C2, V8 TurboFan, JVM), the analogous mechanism is **inline caches (ICs)**: a call site caches the last-seen receiver type; a monomorphic IC that stays monomorphic across invocations is converted by the JIT into a direct, inlinable call guarded by a receiver-type check — a **monomorphic inline cache**; if multiple types recur, the IC becomes **polymorphic** (a small dispatch chain) and inlining of multiple stubs with per-type guards may occur (**polymorphic inlining**), falling back to a **megamorphic** full dispatch when type diversity is too high to profitably specialize. If the speculative assumption is later violated at runtime, the JIT performs **deoptimization**, discarding the optimized/inlined frame and resuming in an interpreter or lower-tier compiled version — this is the dynamic analogue of the guard-failure path in guarded devirtualization.

**Recursive inlining limits**: covered above — bounded by inline history/duplication counters and recursion-depth parameters, since a single recursive function could otherwise be inlined into itself without termination.

## Interaction with other optimizations

Inlining is primarily an *enabling* transformation. After substituting actual arguments for formals, **sparse conditional constant propagation (SCCP)** and local constant folding can eliminate branches whose condition becomes a compile-time constant; **dead code elimination (DCE)** then removes the now-unreachable blocks and any callee-internal computation whose result became dead given the specific call-site arguments. Inlining also exposes **aliasing information** (callee's pointer parameters are now known to alias or not alias specific caller-side objects), enabling more precise **alias analysis** and therefore more aggressive **load/store forwarding**, **LICM**, and **scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA)**. Because these downstream passes are often what make inlining profitable in practice (rather than the raw call-overhead elimination), production pass pipelines iterate: inline, run a cleanup pipeline (SROA, instcombine/GVN, SCCP, DCE), and re-run the inliner on the simplified call graph (LLVM's `CGSCCPassManager` wraps a function simplification pipeline inside the SCC inlining iteration for exactly this reason). The fundamental trade-off remains code size (I-cache footprint, binary size, compile time) versus runtime speed (eliminated call/return overhead, saved register spills around call sites, and — most importantly — the unlocked downstream optimizations), which is why `-Os`/`-Oz` thresholds are far more conservative than `-O2`/`-O3`.

---

# Loop Vectorization

## SLP vectorization vs. loop-level vectorization

These are two distinct units of parallelism discovery that are often confused:

**Loop-level (loop) vectorization** takes a single scalar loop performing the same operation across iterations and transforms it to operate on a vector of W consecutive iterations per iteration of a new, shorter loop — exploiting **data-level parallelism across loop iterations**. This is the domain of the **LLVM Loop Vectorizer** (`LoopVectorize.cpp`) and **GCC's tree-vectorizer's loop-vectorization pass** (`tree-vect-loop.c`).

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization**, originally from Larsen & Amarasinghe's 2000 PLDI paper, instead finds **isomorphic, independent scalar operations within straight-line code** (potentially across a single loop iteration body, or even outside any loop, e.g., repeated struct-field arithmetic) and packs them into a single vector instruction. It builds a "pack" of isomorphic instructions by following use-def chains from a seed of adjacent memory accesses (e.g., consecutive array stores) and groups operations level-by-level. LLVM's **SLPVectorizer** pass and GCC's **basic-block vectorizer** (`tree-vect-slp.c`, often referred to as BB-SLP) implement this. Critically, SLP operates at the basic-block/straight-line level and does not require any loop restructuring, whereas loop vectorization must restructure loop control flow (trip count, induction variables, remainder handling). In modern pipelines the two are complementary and often run in sequence: the Loop Vectorizer vectorizes across iterations, and the SLP vectorizer then additionally packs any remaining isomorphic scalar work within the vectorized loop body (e.g., in the unrolled-and-jammed segments) or handles loops the Loop Vectorizer declined to touch.

## Legality and profitability analysis

**Legality** hinges on proving the absence of vectorization-blocking dependences. The compiler builds **data dependence graphs** for memory references in the loop body using a **dependence testing** framework, classically formalized via **distance vectors** and **direction vectors** over the iteration space (per Allen & Kennedy / Wolfe's loop dependence theory). For a pair of array references across loop iterations, the dependence test (e.g., the **GCD test**, **Banerjee test**, or exact tests for affine subscripts) determines whether a dependence exists, and if so its **distance** (number of iterations separating dependent accesses) and **direction** (`<`, `=`, `>`, or `*` if indeterminate). A dependence with distance ≥ vector width and consistent direction is vectorizable (loop-carried dependence spans more than one vector group); a dependence with distance 0 across the vectorized dimension, or an indeterminate direction, is generally vectorization-blocking unless resolved by **loop versioning** with a runtime disambiguation check. LLVM's Loop Vectorizer uses `LoopAccessAnalysis`/`MemoryDepChecker`, which attempts to prove bounded/no dependence via SCEV (scalar evolution) analysis of array subscripts, and failing a static proof, can emit **runtime pointer-aliasing checks** (a form of **loop versioning for vectorization**, as distinct from versioning for alignment) that branch to a scalar fallback if pointers turn out to actually overlap. GCC's tree-vectorizer performs the analogous analysis via `vect_analyze_data_refs` and `vect_analyze_dependences`, also able to insert runtime alias checks.

**Profitability** is governed by a **cost model**: the compiler estimates the cost of the vectorized loop body (instruction count weighted by target-specific per-instruction vector costs from `TargetTransformInfo` in LLVM, or `targetm.vectorize.builtin_vectorization_cost` in GCC) against the scalar loop cost, factoring in expected **vector width** (VF, the vectorization factor), **unroll/interleave factor** (UF, additional scalar-equivalent unrolling folded into the vector loop to hide latency and improve instruction-level parallelism), and overheads (vector setup, remainder loop, masking cost, gather/scatter cost for non-unit-stride accesses, horizontal reduction cost). The Loop Vectorizer iterates candidate VFs (e.g., 2, 4, 8 for a given element type and target vector register width, as well as scalable vector factors for SVE/RVV) and selects the VF×UF combination with the lowest estimated cost per element, consulting `LoopVectorizationCostModel::selectVectorizationFactor`.

## Reductions, alignment, strip-mining, and masking

**Reductions**: operations like sum/max/min across loop iterations create an apparent loop-carried dependence (the accumulator), but are recognized as a **reduction idiom** when the combining operator is associative (and, for strict floating-point semantics, must be explicitly permitted to reassociate via `-ffast-math`/`#pragma clang fp reassociate`). The vectorizer maintains a **vector of partial sums** (one lane per SIMD lane) during the vectorized loop body and emits a **horizontal reduction** (e.g., `llvm.vector.reduce.add`, lowered to a shuffle-and-add tree, or a target reduction instruction) after the loop to combine lanes into the final scalar result. LLVM's `RecurrenceDescriptor` and GCC's reduction-recognition in `tree-vect-loop.c` identify these phi-node-rooted patterns explicitly.

**Loop peeling and versioning for alignment**: many ISAs either require or strongly prefer aligned vector loads/stores. If the loop's base pointer alignment is not statically known to be a multiple of the vector width, the compiler can **peel** a small prologue of scalar iterations to advance the pointer to an aligned boundary before entering the vectorized main loop, or perform **loop versioning for alignment**: generate two loop versions (one assuming alignment, with a runtime check on the pointer's low bits dispatching to it; a fallback unaligned/scalar version otherwise). LLVM's `LoopVectorizer`/`LoopAccessAnalysis` and GCC's `vect_do_peeling` implement these as concrete, named transformations.

**Strip-mining and the remainder loop**: loop vectorization is a specific case of **strip-mining** — partitioning the original iteration space into strips of size VF — producing a **vectorized main loop** processing full VF-sized chunks, and a **scalar remainder (epilogue) loop** handling the trip-count-mod-VF leftover iterations that don't fill a complete vector. Both LLVM and GCC emit this remainder loop by default; LLVM can alternatively **vectorize the epilogue with a smaller VF** (epilogue vectorization) to reduce residual scalar overhead, and for statically known trip counts divisible by VF, the remainder loop can be elided entirely.

**Predicated/masked vectorization**: for loops with data-dependent control flow (if/else inside the loop body), rather than refusing to vectorize, the compiler performs **if-conversion**, transforming control flow into data flow via **select instructions** or **masked (predicated) memory operations** (masked load/store/gather/scatter), where a per-lane boolean mask (derived from the branch condition, computed as a vector compare) determines which lanes actually commit their effect. This is essential both for divergent control flow in traditional SIMD loops and is the same fundamental mechanism underlying **SIMT execution on GPUs** (where every "thread" in a warp/wavefront executes with an implicit per-lane predicate mask for divergent branches, and reconvergence occurs when masks merge back). LLVM's Loop Vectorizer performs if-conversion via `LoopVectorizationLegality::canVectorizeWithIfConversion` and generates masked intrinsics (`llvm.masked.load`/`store`/`gather`/`scatter`) consumed by the backend; explicit mask control is also exposed via **VP (vector-predicated) intrinsics** and length-based predication for scalable vector ISAs (ARM SVE's whilelt-based predicate generation, RISC-V V extension's vl/vtype).

## Reference implementations and vector width selection

The **LLVM Loop Vectorizer** targets `TargetTransformInfo`-reported preferred/maximum vector register widths and emits IR-level vector types (`<4 x float>`, or scalable `<vscale x 4 x float>` for SVE/RVV), leaving final instruction selection to the backend. **GCC's tree-vectorizer** (part of the GIMPLE "tree-ssa" pipeline, invoked via `-ftree-vectorize`, implied by `-O3`) performs an analogous GIMPLE-level transformation producing vector-typed GIMPLE statements lowered during RTL expansion. Both support **multiple vectorization factors per target** (e.g., choosing between 128-bit SSE, 256-bit AVX2, 512-bit AVX-512 on x86, selected by `-march`/target-attribute-driven cost tables) and both expose vectorization diagnostics (`-Rpass=loop-vectorize` / `-fopt-info-vec-missed`) used to explain missed-optimization reasons tied back to the legality/cost analysis above.

---

# General Loop Optimizations

## Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM hoists computations whose operands do not change across loop iterations out of the loop body, into the loop's **preheader** — a dedicated single-entry block executed exactly once before the loop, which both LLVM (`LoopSimplify`) and GCC guarantee exists as part of loop-normalized form specifically to give LICM (and other loop passes) a safe, canonical hoist target.

Correctness requires two separate properties beyond "the value doesn't change": **control dependence/dominance safety** — the hoisted instruction must be guaranteed to execute on every path through the loop that originally reached it, which is why LICM requires the candidate instruction to be in a block that **dominates all loop exits** (or more precisely, hoisting is safe outright for a block that dominates the loop latch/all exiting blocks, and otherwise requires the instruction to be provably **speculatable**, i.e., side-effect-free and not trapping, since hoisting an instruction to a point that always executes when the original executed only conditionally can introduce a fault — e.g., a division by a loop-invariant divisor that happened to be zero on paths not actually reached — this is why LICM in LLVM uses `isSafeToExecuteUnconditionally`/`isGuaranteedToExecute`). The second property is **memory safety**: hoisting a load or sinking a store across iterations requires alias analysis to prove no other memory operation in the loop (or in an aliasing-unclear callee) can write to the same location, formalized in LLVM via `MemorySSA`-based LICM, which hoists/sinks `MemoryUse`/`MemoryDef` instances only when no intervening clobbering `MemoryDef` exists in the loop. **Exception safety** matters for languages/targets with precise exception semantics: hoisting an instruction that may throw (or trap, e.g., an integer divide) above a point where, originally, an earlier-in-program-order exception might have fired first, can change observable exception ordering, so compilers either restrict hoisting to provably non-throwing/non-trapping instructions or require the hoist target to be proven to preserve exception order.

## Induction variable analysis and strength reduction

An **induction variable (IV)** is a variable whose value forms an arithmetic (or more generally affine/polynomial) progression across loop iterations. The **basic induction variable** is typically the loop counter (incremented by a constant each iteration); **derived (linear) induction variables** are variables defined as an affine function of a basic IV (`j = a*i + b`). **Induction variable analysis**, formalized in LLVM via **Scalar Evolution (SCEV)**, represents each such variable symbolically as a **chain of recurrences** (CIR), e.g., `{start,+,step}<loop>`, enabling closed-form reasoning about a variable's value at any iteration without simulating the loop.

**Strength reduction** replaces an expensive operation on a derived IV (e.g., multiplication, as in an array-indexing computation `base + i*4`) with cheaper operations by maintaining the derived value incrementally via addition of the step each iteration, rather than recomputing it from the basic IV each time — turning a per-iteration multiply into a per-iteration add. This is classically paired with **induction variable elimination**: once all uses of a basic or derived IV have been rewritten in terms of a single canonical IV (or the pointer-based IV used directly for address computation), the original now-redundant IVs are deleted. LLVM implements this as the dedicated **`IndVarSimplify`** pass (canonicalizes IVs, often introducing a canonical `{0,+,1}` IV and widening/narrowing IVs as needed) in conjunction with the lower-level **LSR (Loop Strength Reduction)** pass, which specifically targets address-computation strength reduction, choosing which IVs to keep live based on a target-aware cost model (accounting for addressing-mode support, e.g., whether the target ISA supports scaled-index addressing natively, in which case strength-reducing a multiply may be counterproductive). GCC's equivalent is the **IVOPTS (induction variable optimizations)** pass (`tree-ssa-loop-ivopts.c`), which performs IV candidate selection, cost-based selection of a minimal set of IVs to materialize, and elimination of redundant ones.

## Unrolling, fusion, fission, interchange, tiling, and the polyhedral model

**Loop unrolling** replicates the loop body N times per iteration of a shortened loop (reducing trip count by factor N), amortizing per-iteration overhead (branch, induction variable increment/comparison) and exposing more instructions for **instruction scheduling** and **instruction-level parallelism**; it may be full (eliminating the loop entirely for a statically known small trip count) or partial, and is frequently paired with a remainder/epilogue loop analogous to the vectorization remainder discussed above. LLVM's `LoopUnrollPass` and GCC's `cunroll`/`cunrolli` passes use heuristics based on estimated code growth, estimated cycle savings, and whether unrolling enables further simplification (e.g., constant-folding array accesses with now-constant indices).

**Loop fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into a single loop body, improving data locality (if both loops touch the same data, fusion keeps it in cache/registers across what were two separate passes) and amortizing loop overhead, but is only legal when it does not introduce a new dependence violation (specifically, no statement in the second loop may depend on a later iteration's value from the first loop than fusion would preserve — checked via dependence distance/direction analysis as in vectorization). **Loop fission (distribution)** is the inverse: splitting one loop into multiple loops each handling a subset of the original body's statements, which can be necessary to enable vectorization of the vectorizable portion while leaving a non-vectorizable statement (e.g., one with a non-affine dependence) in a separate scalar loop — LLVM's `LoopDistribute` pass performs exactly this, splitting loops specifically to unblock the Loop Vectorizer on the distributable part.

**Loop interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loops in a loop nest (exchanging outer and inner loop headers), primarily to improve **spatial locality** by making the innermost loop stride over the dimension that corresponds to contiguous memory layout (e.g., row-major array access should have the row index as the innermost loop), reducing cache misses; legality again requires dependence analysis — specifically the dependence direction vector must remain "forward" (lexicographically non-negative) after interchange, or interchange would reorder dependent accesses illegally. **Loop tiling (blocking)** partitions a loop nest's iteration space into smaller rectangular (or other shaped) blocks sized to fit a cache level's working set, trading increased loop-nest control overhead for dramatically improved reuse within each tile — a cornerstone transformation for dense linear algebra (matrix multiply tiling for register/L1/L2 reuse). These multi-loop-nest transformations (interchange, tiling, skewing, fusion under complex dependence patterns) are most rigorously handled via the **polyhedral model**: representing a loop nest's iteration domain, dependences, and schedule as integer polyhedra and affine maps, then searching for a legal affine schedule transformation (via tools/frameworks such as **Pluto**, **ISL (Integer Set Library)**, and **Polly** for LLVM, or GCC's **Graphite** infrastructure) that optimizes an objective (locality, parallelism) while mechanically guaranteeing dependence preservation through the mathematics of the affine scheduling rather than ad hoc pattern-matching on direction vectors.

## Canonical form: LCSSA, normalization, and guard hoisting

**Loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA)** requires that every value defined inside a loop that is used outside the loop have that use mediated through a **phi node in the loop's exit block**, even if there is only a single predecessor — effectively giving every "loop-carried-out" value a single, uniform access point. This simplifies many loop transformations (LICM, unrolling, vectorization, loop interchange) because they no longer need to reason about arbitrary use sites scattered throughout the post-loop code; they only need to update the exit-block phi. LLVM materializes this explicitly as the `LCSSA` pass, required as a precondition by most loop passes in its pipeline.

**Loop normalization/canonicalization** encompasses a family of shape-regularizing transformations performed before substantive loop optimization: ensuring a single **preheader** block, a single **latch** (the block containing the back-edge to the header), simplifying the loop to have a recognizable **canonical induction variable**, and rotating the loop into **loop-rotate (do-while) form** — transforming a `while`-style loop (test-then-body) into a `do...while`-style loop with the exit test at the bottom (after an initial guard check), which both simplifies LICM/unrolling (one test per iteration instead of two) and is a prerequisite many vectorizer/unroller implementations rely on. LLVM's `LoopSimplify` and `LoopRotate` passes perform exactly this normalization; GCC's loop infrastructure (`cfgloop`) maintains analogous invariants.

**Loop-invariant guard hoisting** hoists a loop-invariant conditional check (a "guard" — e.g., a null-check, bounds-check, or type-check that is re-evaluated identically every iteration because its operands don't change) out of the loop body, converting a per-iteration branch into a single pre-loop branch (potentially combined with loop versioning: hoist the guard, and if it would fail, branch to a slow/safe fallback path instead of executing the optimized loop at all). This is especially significant in managed-language JITs (e.g., array bounds-check elimination/hoisting in the JVM's C2 compiler or .NET RyuJIT) where redundant per-iteration safety checks are common and their removal is often a prerequisite for subsequent vectorization, since vectorizers generally refuse to vectorize loops containing not-yet-hoisted trapping conditional checks.
